analysis: Literature in translation, myth, rhetoric, philosophy, empire, Greek archaeology and ancient-democracy heritage form a classical-culture core. Visual history and comparative adaptation add ways to examine reception; original Greek and Latin philology remains outside the composition.

Greek Archaeology and Heritage & Ancient Democracy supply direct material and textual cases for community decision-making, exclusion and citizenship. Political philosophy, ancient and later empires, myth, material history and the Renaissance add historical comparisons. Comparative politics and public law supply structured later cases. Private law, modern history and conflict courses serve as supporting comparisons, without being claimed as courses in Roman law or ancient warfare.

Antiquity, democracy & the politics of t: examines how Western thinkers from the classical political philosophers onward theorised political authority and the good community, which is the question this programme carries into the present
studies the archaeology of community and collective decision-making in early-democratic Greece, giving this programme its material evidence for how an ancient democracy actually worked

reconstructs how Athenian democracy was built, how ancient commentators attacked it as too inclusive and too emotional, and how that contested heritage has been reused since, which is this programme's central case
examines how empires rise, hold and lose power, placing Rome alongside later imperial formations that invoked it
shows how myths of political power, war and community travel and change across cultures
develops independent historical inquiry and source criticism through modern history, as a supporting method for evaluating later uses of the past
examines Renaissance Italian visual culture in Mediterranean and wider exchange, adding a historical context for the transmission of inherited forms

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Academic writing, evidence literacy, presentation and reflective development support the common foundation; these skills support humanities inquiry.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.contribution: sets out legal, social and normative perspectives on law and surveys constitutional, criminal, international and private law, giving the legal vocabulary this programme needs

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.contribution: surveys the modern period from 1815, the era in which popular sovereignty, nationalism and classical political models were argued over in the terms the programme examines

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.contribution: examines the rise, organisation and fall of major empires, including Rome, and the theories used to explain imperial power

GOSHIST213.name: Ways of War
GOSHIST213.contribution: traces warfare in the western world from Greek hoplites and Roman legionnaires onward, covering the military organisation of the ancient societies studied in the cultural-history strand

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.contribution: develops source criticism and independent historical research through a modern history topic

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.contribution: examines human rights both as positive law and as a historical and philosophical construction, the modern counterpart of ancient arguments about who belongs to a political community

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.contribution: covers the sources of international law together with the use of force, armed conflict and refugee law, the contemporary legal frame for questions of movement and membership

GOSLAWJ213.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
GOSLAWJ213.contribution: compares how five constitutional orders establish government, sovereign powers and civil rights, giving the comparative method for reading ancient constitutional arrangements

GOSLAWJ311.name: Principles of Private Law
GOSLAWJ311.contribution: compares property, tort and contract across contemporary legal systems as a supporting contrast in how societies organise rights and obligations

GOSPHIL111.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
GOSPHIL111.contribution: introduces the Western philosophical tradition from the ancient Greeks onward, supplying the ancient philosophical material and the argumentative technique the programme builds on

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: works through virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism from their historical sources, including the ancient ethical theories read in the philosophy strand

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.contribution: examines how influential Western thinkers theorised human nature, society and political authority, beginning with the classical political philosophers

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.contribution: supplies the analytical tools for comparing political systems and explaining how they function and change

GOSPOLI212.name: Theory of International Relations
GOSPOLI212.contribution: introduces the schools of international-relations theory and applies them to historical and contemporary cases of power between polities

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.contribution: examines how a composite political order exercises public authority and turns competing interests into policy

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: examines the causes and dynamics of violent and nonviolent conflict and the conditions for lasting peace across history, sociology, political science and law

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: trains qualitative research design, fieldwork and interpretive data analysis for studying how people make sense of their social and political world

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.contribution: teaches classical rhetorical theory and practice from Plato, Aristotle and Quintilian and the construction of persuasive argument

MCCCOMM211.name: Style & Meaning
MCCCOMM211.contribution: uses grammatical and stylistic evidence to explain interpretive effects in literary and nonfiction texts

MCCCOMM213.name: Rhetoric in Action
MCCCOMM213.contribution: puts classical rhetorical theory into practice through public speaking, debate and storytelling in a community-engaged setting

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.contribution: extends classical rhetoric and argumentation theory into contemporary models of framing and persuasion across public discourse

MCCCOMM312.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
MCCCOMM312.contribution: combines lyric forms, performance and creative writing with reflection on inherited conventions

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.contribution: traces Western art from the early Renaissance onward, the period in which classical forms and subjects were deliberately revived, and trains visual analysis

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.contribution: introduces the material culture of ancient societies from the Near East to classical Athens and Rome, reading artefacts and production techniques as evidence about the communities that made them

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.contribution: studies Renaissance Italian art and its connections through Mediterranean and wider exchange, providing context for the later life of classical forms

MCCHEAM213.name: Greek Archaeology
MCCHEAM213.contribution: studies the archaeology of community and political decision-making in early-democratic Greece directly from its material remains

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.contribution: reconstructs how Athenian democracy was built and how it was expressed in myth, religion, art, literature and architecture, and traces how that heritage was later remembered

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.contribution: examines how a humanities discipline writes its own history and trains art-historical research, visual analysis and academic writing

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.contribution: develops practical criticism and literary interpretation, establishing the formal analysis of literary texts that the programme applies to classical material

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.contribution: surveys canonical literary works chronologically from the epic of Gilgamesh onward, including the ancient texts that shaped the Western literary tradition

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.contribution: compares ancient Greek and Roman myth and epic with other traditions and tests how narrative forms travel between cultures

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.contribution: analyses how literary texts are reworked in a different medium, giving concrete method for studying the afterlife of canonical narratives

MCCLITR312.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
MCCLITR312.contribution: uses contrasting interpretive theories in an independent literary research project

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.contribution: analyses pre-digital media objects, including early printed books, and how their material properties shaped the production, circulation and preservation of knowledge

alignment.rationale: UCR offers no ancient Greek language acquisition or original-language reading sequence.
UCR offers no Latin language acquisition or original-language reading sequence.
UCR has no continuation course in Greek and Latin language acquisition and reading.
UCR has no advanced combined Greek and Latin language course in philosophical and rhetorical prose.
UCR has no Latin linguistics course.
UCR has no Greek linguistics course.
Both study classical literary genres and contextualise ancient texts. UCR includes epic and Greek tragedy in a much wider survey in translation.
Both study ancient epic, myth and interpretation. UCR compares Greek and other narrative traditions in translation; UvA requires close reading and translation of Homer.
Both require advanced humanities interpretation and independent written research; UCR provides a literary research project rather than a Classics term paper.
UCR reads Virgil in translation but has no Latin-language epic course.
UCR has no original-language course in late-antique and medieval Latin literature.
UCR has no original-language course in late-antique and medieval Greek literature.
UCR has no Latin lyric course in the original language.
UCR reads Greek tragedy in translation as part of a wider survey. UvA provides a dedicated Euripides, translation and reception course.
UCR develops creative practice and studies adaptation in separate courses. UvA combines this work specifically with the reception of Greek and Latin texts.
Both study Rome and imperial power. UCR compares Roman and other empires; UvA also follows Hellenistic and Italian cultures through texts and material evidence.
Both teach source criticism through historical investigation. UCR applies it to modern history; UvA focuses on sources for classical antiquity.
Both interpret the ancient Near East and Greek world through cultural and material evidence; UCR embeds them in a global archaeological survey.
Both examine how ancient places and objects acquire later meaning. UCR studies the contested heritage of Athenian democracy.
Both examine humanities knowledge and disciplinary interpretation; UCR does so through the historiography and practice of art history.
UCR has no compulsory ACASA excursion or equivalent credited field component.
UCR has no dedicated Greek-and-Latin historiography course based on original-language texts.
Both introduce ancient philosophical arguments; UCR continues through the wider Western philosophical tradition.
This is genuine approved profiling and has no fixed subject content to align.
The comparator requires an independent Greek and Latin Language and Culture thesis; UCR’s comparison-only optional research element is placed here.

academicConstruction: Rhetoric in Action is unavailable in term four. Swap it with Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean from term six, preserving the first option course set and the art history foundation before Renaissance study. The second option replaces European Union Law with Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean to expand the historical and material context and reduce overlap with European Union Politics. The programmes retain seven and six advanced units, and differ by 11 courses and 82.5 EC in each direction. Screened active language, literature, philosophy and archaeological material. The original-language candidate has no sequenced Greek and Latin grammar, translation, philology or primary-language seminars, regardless of term availability.
